data.name: Zap Zap Zombie Cats
data.detailed_description:
You are one of the few survivors of a zombie cat-pocalypse. With only your wits, your weapons, and a few turrets, you must defend yourself from the hordes of zombie-cats that come at night. Grenade, blast, shoot, heal, and place traps to survive each wave until safety comes with the sunlight.

This is Zap Zap Zombie Cats. A mix between a turret defense game and an FPS. Gameplay is split into two parts: a day portion where you must build and upgrade various turrets during the day to prepare for the night invasion, and a night portion where you take place in the action from a stationary position atop your base. During this stage, you can switch between 3 various cats, each with a different weapon and ability to utilize against the horde.

Zap Zap was made from a team of college students looking to gain experience and learn about the game-making process. We know the game won't be perfect, but we hope to improve our skills and greatly appreciate any and all feedback from players.

Features:
3 Characters, each with their own unique weapon and ability,
8 Different enemies,
13 Turret types,
3 levels of upgrade per turret,
and 10 levels with a tutorial and boss stage

reviews.review:
"Zap Zap Zombie Cats" is a student project self-published on Steam Direct. Student projects might look better than amateur shovelware, but they aren't real games. This is just a glorified homework assignment. It lacks the depth and value you get from professionally developed product because it was made for a grade, not for players.

Schools, colleges and universities shouldn't be using Steam to show off student projects. It might be fine for the school's marketing, but it clutters the Steam store with pollution... we have to sort past all these short student tech demos just so we can find real, full games from professional developers.  This is a case of a game dev college putting its own interests before the interests of gamers.

In this case the students made a simple and pointless tech demo... a basic TD/wave survival hybrid where you place stuff, then go through a wave survival shooter supported by the stuff you placed to kill a bunch of zombie cats.  It's not the worst I've ever seen (and I've seen some garbage) but it's very close to the bottom in terms of quality and value... despite being "free". 

In terms of visuals, this features fairly low quality low poly 3D graphics which will deter a lot of gamers, understandably.  Gaming is a visual medium, and while some developers struggle with creating high quality visuals, failing to do so is a disservice to gamers.  It's very difficult to recommend bad looking games.

This game is fairly dated at 8 years old... and even back then it looked old and busted compared to contemporary, professionally made 3D games of the same period.  It looked bad then, it looks worse now.

Let's talk about pricing and the actual value this has for gamers.

It would be unethical for students to try charge money for their homework assignments, so you don't have to pay any money for this.  But you'd still have to spend your time downloading this, and "time is money", as they say.

There's the other problem, too... as a student project, this wasn't made for gamers. There's no requirement for them to polish and balance the game properly, all they need is something to show the faculty so they can get their grade and move on.  Let's once more ask... why is that good for gamers?

It's obviously not delivering a solid product.  Yet here it is, on the store page, and here you are, reading my review for a student demo that's going to waste your time.  While genuine amateur developers who made real products get ignored because they have to compete with this stuff.

In some ways, this deluge of student projects on Steam is harmful to everyone.

You can always judge a game by how popular it is with the general public.  Steam has over 130 million unique gamers, and over 40 million unique logons every day from dedicated PC gamers.  But this only ever had a peak player count of a dozen or so people... that's very poor public reception.  Gamers rejected this, most likely due to the reasons I supply in this review.

Keep in mind this student project won't increase your game collector count or show up in your Steam profile showcases, and because it's a short, unpolished and unmaintained student homework assignment, I can't recommend you spend your valuable time on this one when you could be playing any of the thousands of fully made games for gamers.
